view.stem: Consider an outgoing, small-amplitude mechanical wave in an elastic medium. Which statements describe the wave and the motion of the medium? Select every correct statement.

options.text: The wave is a disturbance that propagates as neighboring particles pass on vibrational motion.
Each particle travels with the disturbance from the source to the far end of the medium.
Particles oscillate locally while the disturbance carries energy through the medium.
The particles remain at rest throughout the passage of the disturbance through the medium.
Every particle begins its motion at the same instant, regardless of its distance from the source.

intent.task: Define the mechanical wave and identify its basic characteristic: propagating vibrational disturbance and energy, with local particle motion rather than material transport. Exact approved n38 definition/model prose is separately bound in en/n38-context.json, blocks 0, 5, 6, 8; the source problems remain n39 problems 1 and 3.
intent.source_solution: An elastically coupled particle passes a disturbance to its neighbor by deformation and force; the neighbor responds with a delay and passes it onward. This is propagation of vibrational motion through the medium. Particles oscillate about their local equilibrium positions rather than traveling with the wave from source to far end. Elastic forces do work on successive particles, so kinetic and elastic potential energy are transmitted. Particle motion is not absent or simultaneous everywhere. These statements describe the approved outgoing, small-amplitude mechanical model, not every electromagnetic wave or nonlinear drift phenomenon.
intent.unit_reason: The definition requested by source 1 and the basic characteristic requested by source 3 are complementary parts of one account of wave motion. A single multiple-selection response requires both the propagation definition and the disturbance-versus-material distinction, avoiding two near-duplicate questions.
limitations: Recognition of the definition and physical distinction does not demonstrate unaided formulation of a definition or explanation in the learner's own words.

rationales.derivation: Displacing a particle deforms its elastic connection; force causes the next particle's delayed motion, and the process repeats. Thus the disturbance propagates by successive transmission of vibration.

Track a moving crest and assign the crest's position to the same material particle at every later time. This substitutes the disturbance trajectory for the particle trajectory and yields transport from source to far end, although the approved particles oscillate locally.
rationales.misconception: Confuse propagation of a wave pattern with bulk travel of the medium by treating a crest as a material particle.

rationales.derivation: Restoring force and inertia produce oscillation around local equilibrium. The elastic coupling does work on neighboring particles, transferring kinetic and elastic potential energy without requiring the material to accompany the disturbance.

Begin with the fact that particles do not accompany the wave to the far end; replace 'no net transport with the wave' by 'no particle motion at all.' This erases the local oscillation required to pass on the disturbance.
rationales.misconception: Infer zero instantaneous motion from absence of transport of the medium with the outgoing wave.

rationales.derivation: Treat all elastic connections as transmitting a displacement instantaneously, ignoring the inertia and successive response delay. Assign every particle the source's start time, which contradicts the delayed outgoing propagation model.
rationales.misconception: Replace finite sequential disturbance transmission with instantaneous response throughout the medium.

view.stem: Which description correctly distinguishes transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves and gives an example of each?

options.text: Transverse: particles oscillate perpendicular to propagation, as in compressions traveling along a spring-connected ball chain. Longitudinal: particles oscillate parallel to propagation, as in side-to-side waves on a taut elastic cord.

Transverse: particles oscillate parallel to propagation, as in side-to-side waves on a taut elastic cord. Longitudinal: particles oscillate perpendicular to propagation, as in compressions traveling along a spring-connected ball chain.

Transverse: particles oscillate parallel to propagation, as in compressions traveling along a spring-connected ball chain. Longitudinal: particles oscillate perpendicular to propagation, as in side-to-side waves on a taut elastic cord.

Transverse: particles oscillate perpendicular to propagation, as in side-to-side waves on a taut elastic cord. Longitudinal: particles oscillate parallel to propagation, as in compressions traveling along a spring-connected ball chain.

intent.task: Compare the relative directions of particle oscillation and wave propagation for both wave types, and match each type with a physical example. Exact n38 prose blocks 0, 5, 6, 8 are separately bound in en/n38-context.json.
intent.source_solution: Transverse waves have particle oscillation perpendicular to propagation; the side-to-side wave along an elastic cord is the approved example. Longitudinal waves have particle oscillation parallel to propagation; the spring-connected chain with compressions and rarefactions is the approved example. The relative directions, rather than the apparatus orientation on the page, define the type.
intent.unit_reason: Both direction comparisons and both examples constitute one classification task. Every alternative supplies a complete two-type account, so the learner cannot satisfy the source by identifying only one type or filling separate direction slots.
limitations: Selecting correctly matched examples does not demonstrate independently generating an example of each type or writing the comparison unaided.

rationales.derivation: Keep the two direction definitions correct but exchange the example assignments. Compression-chain particle motion is parallel, so it cannot instantiate the stated perpendicular transverse definition; side-to-side cord motion is perpendicular, not the stated longitudinal definition.
rationales.misconception: Recall the direction definitions but swap the longitudinal compression-chain and transverse cord examples.

rationales.derivation: Keep the cord labeled transverse and compression chain labeled longitudinal, but exchange the words parallel and perpendicular. The resulting direction claims contradict the motion in both examples.
rationales.misconception: Keep the example names while reversing the relative-direction definitions.

rationales.derivation: Take the physically consistent pair 'parallel motion with compression chain' and label it transverse; take 'perpendicular motion with sideways cord wave' and label it longitudinal. This exchanges the wave-type names for the two complete classifications.
rationales.misconception: Swap the names transverse and longitudinal while retaining each physical direction/example pair.

rationales.derivation: A cord's sideways displacement is perpendicular to travel along the cord. In a compression chain, balls move along the chain, parallel to the propagating compression pattern. Both direction definitions and both examples therefore agree.

view.stem: For a periodic traveling wave, which statement defines its wavelength?

options.text: The distance along propagation between any two distinct points that oscillate in the same phase.
The distance along propagation between the nearest distinct points that oscillate in the same phase.
The maximum distance that one particle is displaced from its equilibrium position during an oscillation.
The distance along propagation between the nearest distinct points that oscillate in opposite phase.

intent.task: Identify wavelength as the fundamental spatial repetition length, preserving the nearest-point and equal-phase conditions.
intent.source_solution: The wavelength is the distance along propagation between the nearest distinct in-phase points. In-phase motion includes the oscillation stage and direction, not just a displacement at one instant. More distant in-phase points can be separated by 2lambda or another integral multiple; nearest antiphase points are lambda/2 apart. The maximum local displacement is amplitude, not wavelength.
intent.unit_reason: One complete-definition judgment distinguishes the fundamental spatial repeat from three concrete alternatives without turning definition clauses into separate yes/no slots.
limitations: Recognition of the complete wavelength definition does not demonstrate unaided recall and formulation of that definition.

rationales.derivation: Retain the equal-phase condition but discard 'nearest.' Choose two crests separated by two full spatial repeats; they are in phase and this procedure assigns 2lambda as wavelength, so it does not define the fundamental wavelength.
rationales.misconception: Remove the nearest-point condition and treat an arbitrary integral multiple of wavelength as the wavelength itself.

rationales.derivation: The oscillation phase repeats by 2pi over one fundamental spatial cycle. The nearest distinct in-phase points mark precisely that cycle, which is the wavelength.
Measure one particle's largest displacement from equilibrium instead of the separation of two points along propagation. This procedure returns the amplitude A, not the wavelength lambda.
rationales.misconception: Use local maximum oscillatory displacement as the spatial repeat length.

rationales.derivation: Use a pi phase change as one full repeat instead of 2pi. This measures lambda/2 between nearest antiphase points, half the wavelength.
rationales.misconception: Substitute opposite phase for equal phase, counting a half-cycle as a full spatial cycle.

view.stem: For a periodic traveling wave, $v$ is wave speed, $\lambda$ is wavelength, $T$ is the vibration period, and $\nu$ is vibration frequency. Which relationship is correct?

options.text: $v=\dfrac{\lambda}{T}=\lambda\nu$
$v=\dfrac{T}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1}{\lambda\nu}$
$v=\lambda T=\dfrac{\lambda}{\nu}$
$v=\dfrac{2\lambda}{T}=2\lambda\nu$

intent.task: Relate wave speed to wavelength and the vibration period/frequency, with both equivalent forms of the relationship.
intent.source_solution: The traveling wave advances lambda during one period T. Its speed is distance/time = lambda/T. Substituting nu = 1/T gives v = lambda*nu. This applies to both transverse and longitudinal waves. Proportionality to wavelength requires holding frequency fixed; the item does not claim a source-frequency change alters the speed of a fixed medium.
intent.unit_reason: A complete symbolic relationship preserves the source's physical relation in both temporal and frequency forms. It is not a cell-by-cell numerical substitution exercise.
limitations: Recognition of the complete relationship does not demonstrate unaided statement of the law or an independently written derivation.

rationales.derivation: One wavelength is traversed in one period, so v = lambda/T; using nu = 1/T gives v = lambda*nu.
Reverse the speed quotient to time/distance: v_wrong = T/lambda. Substitute T = 1/nu to obtain 1/(lambda*nu), the reciprocal of the physical speed.
rationales.misconception: Invert distance divided by time, mistaking the reciprocal speed for speed.

rationales.derivation: Start with distance lambda and elapsed time T but multiply instead of dividing: v_wrong = lambda*T. Substitute T = 1/nu to obtain lambda/nu. The units are length*time rather than speed.
rationales.misconception: Multiply travel distance by duration instead of dividing by duration.

rationales.derivation: Assign one entire wavelength to each of the outward and return halves of a particle's oscillation. Add those two assigned distances to obtain 2lambda per period T, then substitute 1/T = nu. This improperly replaces wave-pattern advance by an invented particle round-trip distance.
rationales.misconception: Count the outward and return halves of local oscillation as two full wavelength advances in one period.

view.stem: In Figure 70, what is the smallest phase-difference magnitude, in radians, between two neighboring balls after the wave has reached both?

options.text: $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$\dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

intent.task: Infer the phase increment across adjacent balls from the full approved Figure 70. The separately bound n38 context block 7 establishes that panel spacing is T/4 and arrows show velocity.
intent.source_solution: Panel e marks one wavelength from the equilibrium position of ball 1 to that of ball 13, giving 13 - 1 = 12 equal neighboring intervals. Panel f independently marks 2-to-14 and 3-to-15 wavelength spans, also 12 intervals. A full wavelength carries a 2pi phase change, hence each neighboring increment has magnitude 2pi/12 = pi/6 radians = 30 degrees, with propagation delay T/12. The farther-along ball lags for the rightward wave. The visible stem asks the unsigned smallest magnitude after both balls have been reached, avoiding the undefined phase of the undisturbed tail.
intent.unit_reason: One neighboring-pair phase calculation is the full written source task. The shared approved image supplies the necessary interval count; the stem does not state that count or the wavelength-to-phase calculation.
limitations: Selecting the phase difference does not demonstrate independently producing the calculation or explaining the lag direction.
The unsigned magnitude and the wave-reached region are made explicit to settle sign and pre-arrival conventions left implicit in the source.

figure_observations.observation: Opened the actual approved SVG as a complete 1280x3060 white-paper rendering, source SHA-256 4bae69e25800526c2b16adca5af0d6c71bb013159e240e6d4474e72cd15fba9f. All panels a-f, balls 1-18, far-right time labels, and both bottom wavelength markers are visible. Panel e marks equilibrium positions 1-to-13; panel f marks 2-to-14 and 3-to-15. Each spans 12 gaps. Untouched tail balls remain at equilibrium before arrival. Full image-open details are in image-open-log.json.

rationales.derivation: Mistake the half-wavelength separation from ball 1 to ball 7 for a full wavelength. Count its six gaps and divide a full-cycle phase 2pi by six: 2pi/6 = pi/3. That separation is only lambda/2, so its phase change is pi, not 2pi.
rationales.misconception: Use the six intervals in a half wavelength as the number of intervals in a full phase cycle.

rationales.derivation: Count the balls numbered 1 through 13 inclusively, giving 13, rather than the 12 gaps between them. Divide the full-cycle phase by this erroneous count to obtain 2pi/13.
rationales.misconception: Count endpoint-inclusive objects instead of the intervals within the marked wavelength.

rationales.derivation: The marked wavelength spans 13 - 1 = 12 equally spaced intervals. Divide the full-cycle phase change 2pi by 12 to obtain pi/6.

Take the T/4 interval between illustrated panels as the vibration delay between neighboring balls. Convert that assumed delay to phase: 2pi*(T/4)/T = pi/2. The spatial wavelength marker instead gives neighboring delay T/12.
rationales.misconception: Confuse the quarter-period sampling interval between panels with the propagation delay between adjacent particles.
